verdict.reasoning: Patient says, “recently I'm wheezy… I have feel like kind of short of breath” and when asked how long, replies “two, three days. Yeah, quite recently.”
Patient reports “I have cough and cough a lot,” but there is no description that it is specifically dry; sputum is denied later, but the term “dry cough” is not used.
When asked, “What was your temperature?” patient replies, “Uh, thirty seven, yeah.”

Dyspnea on exertion: patient says they used to walk to work but recently cannot due to feeling very short of breath. Sentence-splitting: patient says, “sometimes I feel like I can't even finish sentence is quite difficult to… complete the… talking sometimes.”

No sputum/hemoptysis: to “Have you coughed any phlegm up?” patient says “No,” and to “Any… blood in there when you cough?” replies “No, I don't think so.” No chest pain: “Any chest pain?” – “No chest pain, no.” No nocturnal symptoms: to “Have you been woken up at night time at all?” patient answers “No, just daytime working, yeah.”

History of childhood asthma: when asked about problems as a child, patient says “yes, I had asthma.” Severity with hospital visits: Doctor asks, “did you ever have to go to hospital with it?” patient: “Yeah, sometimes.” and “No, not that bad but still, sometimes, need to go to hospital.” This supports significant childhood asthma with hospital visits, though not ICU-level severe.
Patient states, “I also had, uh, hay fever…” and later, to “Any other medical problems?” replies, “Uh, I have, uh, hay fever as well.”
Patient says, “I also had, uh, hay fever and eczema, sorry.”
Patient does use salbutamol (“I took salbutamol… Normally, yeah.”), but there is no mention of increased use in the past 3 days; timing of recent increased use is not discussed.
To “And any allergies to medications?” patient replies, “No, no allergies.”
Smoking: “Do you smoke?” – “No, I don't smoke.” Alcohol: patient says they drink “one glass of wine” and “Every two or three days? Depends, yeah.”
Living situation: “Who do you live with at home?” – “I live with my partner.” Occupation: “what's your job, day-to-day?” – “Uh, I'm engineer.”

Impact on work and walking: patient says they used to walk to work but now “I work from home or sometimes I take sick leave” due to shortness of breath, indicating being off work and not walking because of symptoms.

Doctor states, “it sounds like you've had a flare up of your asthma. It could be triggered by, if there's more pollen around, or… you may have a viral infection, causing it to get worse.” This supports asthma exacerbation likely triggered by viral or pollen.
Patient has hay fever but there is no explicit assessment that allergic rhinitis is ‘uncontrolled’; control status is not discussed.
Eczema is mentioned as part of history but there is no information on current activity or stability.
Doctor advises, “if you increase it so you're taking it two to four puffs, like, every four hours? Initially,” and also prescribes a spacer, implying use via spacer once obtained.
Doctor: “I can prescribe you a peak flow meter… and a spacer to use your inhaler a bit more efficiently, which the pharmacist can show you how you use that when you pick it up.”
Doctor: “when you get the peak flow meter… if you can record a value first thing when you wake up… And in the evening over the next week.”

Doctor says, “it will be a good idea when you're feeling better if we can arrange just a review… You could arrange a review in a week or so,” indicating a follow-up review around one week, likely by phone as earlier stated: “then we can discuss that over the phone.”

Doctor: “if you get a high temperature or your wheezing is getting worse, you need to call us back straightaway so we can just advise you further with that.” This covers worsening wheeze and fever; shortness of breath worsening is implicit in wheezing worsening but not separately named.

Doctor: “the other thing to do would be to take a regular antihistamine. Which you can get from the pharmacy, I can put a on your notes about what to take.” This implies starting a regular (daily) OTC antihistamine for hay fever/allergic rhinitis.

Doctor: “it will be a good idea when you're feeling better if we can arrange just a review, just to see how your asthma is, because we may need to start some other medication for you.” This is a routine asthma review after the acute flare.
